sections.h2: Does every Ohio estate have to go through full probate?
sections.html:
No. Ohio lets a probate court release a small estate from administration, and it provides an even simpler route for the tiniest ones. Which route fits depends on the value of the estate's assets, who inherits, and whether a will exists.

Under R.C. 2113.03, an estate may be released from administration if its assets are worth thirty-five thousand dollars or less. The ceiling is one hundred thousand dollars where the surviving spouse takes everything, either because the will leaves every asset to a spouse named in it, or because there is no valid will and the spouse is entitled to all assets under the intestacy statute.

An interested party applies. The court gives notice to the surviving spouse and heirs, publishes notice in a newspaper of general circulation in the county unless notices are waived or found unnecessary, and, once satisfied, can order personal property delivered and real property transferred to the people entitled to it. If the assets are not all cash and securities with readily known values, an appraiser chosen by the applicant and approved by the court sets the value. The court may also appoint a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers, including those for a sale of real property under R.C. 2127.011.

sections.h2: What is a summary release from administration in Ohio?
sections.html:
R.C. 2113.031 covers the smallest estates. A person who is not the surviving spouse and who paid or is obligated in writing to pay the funeral and burial expenses can apply when the assets do not exceed the lesser of five thousand dollars or those expenses. A surviving spouse can apply when funeral costs were prepaid, or when the spouse paid them, and the assets stay within the support allowance plus up to five thousand dollars for funeral and burial expenses.

The application must be on the form the Ohio Supreme Court prescribes, signed before a notary or a deputy clerk of the probate court, and it must describe every known asset. Vehicle details, bank account numbers and balances, and stock or bond information have to be spelled out. An application for a certificate of transfer goes along with it if the estate holds an interest in real estate, together with the filing fee.

A granted order relieves the estate from administration, directs delivery of personal property with title, and directs transfer of title to any real property interests to the applicant.

sections.h2: Who can sell an inherited Ohio house, and how?
sections.html:
Authority depends on how the estate is handled. When an executor or administrator has been appointed, sales of land follow R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43. Where the will gives the executor a testamentary power of sale, the executor may use those sections or proceed under the will.

Heirs and devisees who receive the house instead take title through a certificate of transfer under R.C. 2113.61. The executor or administrator files the application after the inventory lists the real property and before the final account. It states the decedent's name, domicile and date of death, whether there was a will, why the property is going to the devisees, whether spousal elections, disclaimers or assignments were filed, and that known debts are paid or secured. Within five days after a compliant application, the court issues the certificate for recording in each county where the land lies.

If no administration happens, an heir or devisee can file the application in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived or where the land sits. When an estate is released from administration, the court's transfer order can substitute for the certificate.

sections.h2: How long do creditors have to present claims against an Ohio estate?
sections.html:
Six months from the date of death. Under R.C. 2117.06, all claims must be presented within six months after death, whether or not the estate is released from administration or an executor or administrator is appointed in that period. A claim presented late is forever barred as to all parties, apart from contingent claims handled under R.C. 2117.37 to 2117.42.

Claims go in writing to the executor or administrator, to that person's attorney of record, or to the probate court with the case number on it. After appointment, the executor or administrator allows or rejects a claim within thirty days of presentation, though a late answer does not hurt the claimant.

This matters to anyone planning a quick sale. The statute on small-estate releases says transfers under an order are made subject to the creditor-claim limits in R.C. 2117.06(B) and (C). A court order relieving the estate has the same effect as administration in freeing real property held by an innocent purchaser for value from claims of unsecured creditors.

sections.h2: Can an Ohio owner avoid probate for the house, and what about disclosure and estate tax?
sections.html:
Yes, one route is a transfer on death designation. Under R.C. 5302.22, an owner can record a transfer on death designation affidavit naming beneficiaries. The affidavit is verified before a person authorized to administer oaths, recorded with the county recorder before the owner's death, and needs no consideration and no delivery to the beneficiary. At death, title vests in the beneficiary who survives. A married owner's spouse signs a statement subordinating dower rights.

Disclosure rules matter to a sale from an estate. R.C. 5302.30 exempts transfers ordered by a court, including a probate court, and transfers by a fiduciary in the course of administering an estate. It also exempts a seller who inherited or took by devise and has not lived in the home within the past year. Other sellers of one-to-four unit homes, such as an heir who moved in, must complete the state disclosure form.

On estate tax, R.C. 5731.02 levies the tax on persons dying on or after July 1, 1968 and before January 1, 2013. The levy is limited to those dates.

  • Before any sale, find out which document gives authority: letters from the court, a certificate of transfer, or an order releasing the estate.
  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate needs a commissioner or an appraisal.
  • Ask the title company which recorded papers it wants to see before closing.

faqs.q: What is the Ohio probate limit for a small estate?
faqs.a: Thirty-five thousand dollars or less in assets, or one hundred thousand dollars or less when a surviving spouse takes everything. These figures come from R.C. 2113.03, and the probate court must still enter an order.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims after a death in Ohio?
faqs.a: Six months after the date of death. A claim not presented in that time is barred, with limited exceptions for contingent claims, under R.C. 2117.06.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited Ohio house before probate is finished?
faqs.a: A sale needs someone with authority to convey. That is an appointed executor or administrator, an heir holding a certificate of transfer, or a court-appointed commissioner after a release from administration. Ask the probate court which applies to your estate.

faqs.q: Do I need the Ohio property disclosure form when selling an inherited house?
faqs.a: Not if the transfer is by a fiduciary administering the estate, ordered by a court, or made by an heir or devisee who has not occupied the home within the past year. R.C. 5302.30(B)(2) lists these exemptions.

faqs.q: Does Ohio still have an estate tax?
faqs.a: The levy in R.C. 5731.02 covers deaths before January 1, 2013. Ask the Ohio Department of Taxation about any later-year obligations for a specific estate.
